Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 59, verse 2:

﴿It is He who expelled those who disbelieved﴾ meaning the Banu al-Nadir, ﴿at the first gathering﴾. Regarding its meaning there are four opinions. The first: it is the gathering of the Resurrection, meaning their expulsion from their fortresses is the first gathering, and rising from the graves is the last of it. It is narrated with this meaning that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them: "Proceed, this is the first gathering, and I am behind you in the footsteps." The second: the meaning is that the first place of gathering is the Levant (al-Sham), because most of the Banu al-Nadir went out to the Levant, and it has come in a report that the gathering of the Resurrection is to the land of the Levant. It is narrated with this meaning that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to the Banu al-Nadir: "Go out." They said: "To where?" He said: "To the land of the gathering." The third: the intended gathering is the gathering in this world, which is the exile and expulsion, so He expelled them from their fortresses at the first gathering, and the expulsion of the people of Khaybar was the last of it. The fourth: its meaning is their expulsion from their homes at the first time they were gathered for fighting them, because it was the first battle the Prophet (ﷺ) fought against them. Al-Zamakhshari said: the lam in His saying "li-awwali" means "ʿinda" (at), as when you say "I came at a certain time" (ji'tu li-waqti kadha). ﴿You did not think that they would go out﴾, meaning because of the multitude of their numbers and the strength of their fortresses. ﴿Then Allah came upon them﴾, an expression for Allah's seizing them. ﴿They destroyed their houses with their own hands and the hands of the believers﴾. As for the destruction by the believers, it was the demolition of the fortress walls so that they could enter them, and it was attributed to the disbelievers in His saying "they destroy" because it happened on account of their disbelief and treachery. As for the disbelievers' destruction of their own houses, it was for three purposes: the first, their need for the wood and stones to block the openings of the alleys and to fortify what the Muslims had destroyed of the walls. The second, to carry away with them whatever of the wood and pillars and other things pleased them. The third, so that their dwellings would not remain standing for the Muslims, so they demolished them out of greed for them. ﴿So take warning, O people of insight﴾. Those who affirmed analogical reasoning (qiyas) in jurisprudence cited this verse as evidence, but their argument from it is weak and falls outside its meaning.

﴿Had Allah not decreed for them the exile, He would have punished them in this world﴾. Al-jala' is leaving one's homeland. The meaning is: had Allah not decreed for the Banu al-Nadir their departure from their homelands, He would have punished them in this world by the sword, as He did to their brethren, the Banu Qurayza. Along with that, they have the punishment of the Fire. "شَآقُّواْ" (shaqqu) is mentioned in (Surah) al-Anfal.

﴿Had Allah not decreed for them the exile, He would have punished them in this world﴾. Al-jala' is leaving one's homeland. The meaning is: had Allah not decreed for the Banu al-Nadir their departure from their homelands, He would have punished them in this world by the sword, as He did to their brethren, the Banu Qurayza. Along with that, they have the punishment of the Fire. "شَآقُّواْ" (shaqqu) is mentioned in (Surah) al-Anfal.

﴿What you cut down of the palm trees (līna)﴾. Al-līna is the palm tree (nakhla). It is also said to be the noble kind of palm (al-karīma min al-nakhl), and it is also said to be the palm that is not ʿajwa (a dates variety), and it is also said to be the mixed varieties of palms.

The occasion of revelation was that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) descended upon the fortresses of the Banu al-Nadir, the Muslims cut down some of their palm trees and burned them. The Banu al-Nadir said: "This is nothing but corruption, O Muhammad, and yet you forbid corruption!" So the verse was revealed, informing that whatever was cut down or left standing, Allah had permitted the Muslims to do so. ﴿And that He might disgrace the defiantly disobedient﴾, meaning the Banu al-Nadir.

Some jurists used this verse as evidence that every mujtahid (one who exercises independent legal reasoning, ijtihad) is correct, since Allah has affirmed the action of both the one who cut the palm trees and the one who left them. The scholars differed concerning cutting down the trees of the polytheists and laying waste to their lands. The majority permitted it on the basis of this verse and on the Prophet's (ﷺ) approval of burning the palm trees of the Banu al-Nadir. Others disliked it, on account of the instruction of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) to the army he sent toward al-Sham, that they should not cut down any fruit-bearing tree.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 59, verse 6:

﴿And what Allah restored to His Messenger from them, you did not spur horses or camels for it; but Allah gives authority to His messengers over whom He wills, and Allah is over all things competent.﴾

The meaning of "afa'a Allah" (Allah made it fay' for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ). "Awjaftum" comes from al-wajif, which is rapid travel. Rikab are camels. The meaning is that what Allah gave His Messenger of the wealth of the Banu al-Nadir was not reached by the Muslims on horses or camels, nor did they exert themselves for it, nor did they acquire it by fighting; rather it was obtained by Allah giving His Messenger power over the Banu al-Nadir. Thus Allah informs, through this verse, that what he took from the Banu al-Nadir and what he took from Fadak is fay' specific to the Prophet ﷺ, who disposes of it as he wills, because it was not obtained by rapid pursuit, and no great fighting took place over it. These are unlike the ghanima (spoils of war) which are taken by fighting. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ took for himself from the wealth of the Banu al-Nadir the sustenance of his household, and distributed the rest among the Muhajirun, and gave the Ansar none of it, except that Abu Duhana and Sahl ibn Hunayf complained of poverty, so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ gave them a share of it. This is the view of a group. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to spend from it on his family a year's provision, and what remained he placed in weapons and horses as a provision in the way of Allah.

And some scholars said: Likewise, everything that the rulers (al-a'immah) conquer without rapid pursuit is for them specifically; they take from it what they need and spend the remainder on the public interests of the Muslims.

﴿What Allah restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns belongs to Allah and to the Messenger﴾, and so on, to the end of the verse. People have differed greatly in interpreting this verse and its ruling. Its apparent meaning is that the wealth taken from the disbelievers is for Allah, for the Messenger, and for those mentioned after them, and that no one-fifth (khums) is taken out of it, nor is it divided among those who were present at the encounter. This conflicts with what is stated in al-Anfal about taking out the khums and dividing the rest of the spoils (ghanima, war booty taken by fighting) among those who were present at the encounter. Some of them said: this verse has been abrogated (mansukh) by the verse of al-Anfal. This is an error, because the verse of al-Anfal was revealed a considerable time before this one. Others said: the verse of al-Anfal concerns the wealth taken as spoils other than land, while this verse concerns the land of the disbelievers. They said: for this reason, ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) did not divide the land of Egypt and Iraq, but left it for the benefit of the Muslims. This specification has no evidence to support it. Other views were also expressed. The correct view is that there is no conflict between this verse and the verse of al-Anfal. The verse of al-Anfal concerns the ruling on spoils (ghanima) taken by fighting and by the charging of horses and riding-beasts; from this, the khums is taken out and the remainder is divided among those who took the spoils. As for this verse, it concerns the ruling on fayʾ (wealth obtained without fighting), which is what is taken from property without fighting and without charging with horses or riding-beasts. Given this, each of the two verses has a meaning different from the other and a ruling different from the other, so there is no conflict between them and no abrogation. Observe how the word fayʾ is used here, while the word ghanima is used in al-Anfal. It is established in jurisprudence that there is a difference between fayʾ and ghanima and that their rulings differ. This was stated by Abu Muhammad ibn al-Faras, and it is the view of the majority, and Malik and all his companions held it; it is the most apparent of the opinions.

As for the action of ʿUmar regarding the land of Egypt and Iraq, the correct view is that he did it for the benefit of the Muslims, after the souls of those who took the spoils had been content (with this), based on the words of the Most High: ﴿What Allah restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns﴾. He means without fighting and without charging with horses or riding-beasts, as was the case with the property of Banu al-Nadir. However, the verse omitted this because of His words in the verse before it: ﴿for you did not press on it with horses or riding-beasts﴾. Mentioning that first made it unnecessary to mention it a second time. For this reason, the conjunctive waw (al-waw al-ʿatifa) does not occur at the beginning of this sentence, because it completes the first one and is not separate from it. The first verse explained the ruling on the property of Banu al-Nadir, and this verse explained the ruling on the property of others like it in general. The fayʾ is spent on the same things on which the khums of the spoils is spent, because Allah equated them in His words: ﴿for Allah and the Messenger, and for the kinsfolk, the orphans, the needy and the wayfarer﴾. We have already mentioned this in al-Anfal, so there is no need to repeat it. We have also mentioned in al-Anfal the meaning of His words: ﴿for Allah and the Messenger﴾ and what follows, ﴿so that it does not become a circulating wealth among the rich﴾. That is, so that the fayʾ which Allah restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns does not become a dawla (a circulating benefit) that only the rich benefit from while the poor do not. This is because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) divided the property of Banu al-Nadir among the Muhajirun, since they were poor at that time, and he gave none of it to the Ansar, since they were wealthy. Some of the Ansar said: "We too have our share of this fayʾ." Then Allah revealed this verse. The word dawla, with a damma or a fatha, means what a person circulates with of good, that is, what turns in his favour. It may also come from al-mudawala (taking turns), meaning: so that this wealth does not circulate among the rich, leaving the poor with nothing.

﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾. It was revealed concerning the fayʾ mentioned above. That is: whatever the Messenger gives you of the fayʾ, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it. It is as if it were a command to the Muhajirun to take the fayʾ and a prohibition to the Ansar from it. Nevertheless, the wording of the verse is general, covering the commands or prohibitions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). For this reason, ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud used it as evidence for the prohibition of wearing stitched garments by the one in ihram, and for the curse upon the woman who tattoos and the woman who has false hair added, since this was reported from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

﴿For the poor﴾. This is a substitute (badal) for His words: ﴿and for the kinsfolk, the orphans, the needy and the wayfarer﴾, in order to make clear that what is meant is the Muhajirun. He described them as those who were driven out of their homes and their wealth, because they migrated from Makkah and left their homes and their wealth there.

He described them as those who were driven out of their homes and their wealth, because they migrated from Makkah and left their homes and their wealth there.

﴿And those who had already settled in the abode and in faith before them﴾: these are the Ansar (the Helpers), and the abode is Madinah, because it was their land. The pronoun in "before them" refers to the Muhajirun (the Emigrants).

If it is asked: how can He say "tabawwa'u al-dar wa-al-iman" (settled in the abode and in faith), when one settles in an abode but faith is not settled in? The answer has two aspects. The first is that the meaning is "they settled in the abode and sincerely held to faith." This is like your saying: "I fed it straw (tiban) and cold water (ma'an baridan)," meaning: "I fed it straw and I gave it cold water." The second is that they made faith like a dwelling place for themselves, because they were firmly established in it, just as they made Madinah such a place.

If it is asked: the phrase "from before them" implies that the Ansar preceded the Muhajirun both in settling in Madinah and in faith. As for their precedence in settling in Madinah, there is no doubt about it, since it was their land. As for their precedence in faith, it is problematic, because most of the Muhajirun embraced Islam before the Ansar?

The answer has two aspects. One is that by "from before them" he meant "from before their migration." The other is that he meant "they settled in the abode together with faith," that is, they combined the two conditions before the Muhajirun. For the Muhajirun preceded them only in faith, not in settling in the abode. On this reading, "faith" is an object with "with" (maf'ul ma'ahu). This second aspect is better, because it answers this question and the first question, since if faith is an object with "with," the first question does not arise. It arises only if faith is conjoined (ma'tuf) to "the abode."

﴿And they find in their breasts no need for what they have been given﴾: it has been said that "hajah" (need) here means envy (hasad). It may also mean "need" in its original sense. The pronoun in "they find" refers to the Ansar, and the pronoun in "they have been given" refers to the Muhajirun. The meaning is that the Ansar's souls are content with what the Muhajirun receive from the fay' (spoils) and other things, and they find nothing in their breasts on account of that. ﴿And they prefer [them] over themselves﴾: that is, they prefer others with their wealth over themselves, even when they are in the utmost need, and al-khasasah (poverty, destitution) is al-faqah (indigence).

It is related that the cause of this verse was that when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) divided these villages among the Muhajirun and not the Ansar, he said to the Ansar: "If you wish, you may divide your wealth and your dwellings among the Muhajirun and share this spoil with them; and if you wish, you may keep your wealth and leave these to them." They said: "Rather, we will divide for them from our wealth and leave this spoil to them."

It is also related that its cause was that a man of the Ansar hosted a man of the Muhajirun. The Ansari took the guest to his home, and his wife said to him: "By God, we have nothing but the food of the children." He said to her: "Put your children to sleep, extinguish the lamp, bring out what you have for the guest, and let us show him that we are eating, though we are not eating." They did so. When he went in the morning to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), he said to him: "God was amazed at what you both did last night." Then the verse was revealed: ﴿And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his own soul, those are the successful﴾.

Shuhh al-nafs (the stinginess of the soul) is miserliness and greed. In this there is an indication that God protected the Ansar from the stinginess of their souls, so He praised them for that, and for their preferring others over themselves, and for their finding in their breasts no need for what the Muhajirun were given, and for their loving the Muhajirun.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 59, verse 10:

﴿And those who came after them﴾ This is coordinated with (ma'tuf 'ala) the Muhajirun and the Ansar mentioned before it. The meaning is that the spoils (fay') belong to the Muhajirun and the Ansar, and to those who came after them. By them he means the third group of the Companions, namely those other than the Muhajirun and the Ansar, such as those who embraced Islam on the day of the Conquest (Fath). It has also been said: he means those who came after the Companions, namely the Successors (Tabi'un) and those who follow them until the Day of Resurrection. On this reading Malik interpreted it, and he said: whoever speaks ill of any of the Companions has no share in the booty or the fay', because Allah described those who came after the Companions as saying: ﴿Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith﴾. So whoever says the opposite of that has departed from those whom Allah described.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 59, verses 11–12:

﴿Have you not considered those who played the hypocrite⦆ — the verse: It was revealed concerning ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul and a group of the hypocrites who sent word to the Banu al-Nadir, saying to them: "Stand firm in your fortresses, for we are with you; whatever your circumstances become, we will not obey anyone concerning you, ever." ﴿And we will never obey anyone against you, ever﴾, meaning: we will not listen to the words of any speaker concerning you, nor obey anyone who orders us to abandon you. Then God proved them liars regarding these promises they made.

If it is asked: how does He say "if they were helped, they would surely turn their backs" after saying "they will not be helped"?

The answer: the meaning is by way of supposition and hypothesis, i.e., if we were to suppose that they were helped, they would turn their backs.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 59, verse 13:

﴿Indeed, you are more intimidating in their breasts than Allah﴾ Al-rahba (fear, dread) is khawf (fear), and the meaning is that the hypocrites and the Jews fear people more than they fear Allah.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 59, verse 14:

﴿They will not fight you all together except in fortified towns or from behind walls.﴾ That is, they are not able to fight you as a united body except while they are in fortified towns, protected by ramparts (aswar) and trenches (khandaq), or from behind walls, without coming out to you. ﴿Their violence among themselves is severe.﴾ That is, the enmity of some of them toward others. ﴿You think them united, but their hearts are divided.﴾ That is, you suppose they are gathered together in harmony and affection, while their hearts are scattered by opposition and mutual rancor.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 59, verse 15:

﴿Like those who were before them, not long ago﴾ That is, these Jews are like those who were before them, meaning the Jews of Banu Qaynuqa'. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) expelled them from Madinah before Banu al-Nadir, so they were similar to them. It has been said: it means the disbelievers of the Battle of Badr, for they came before them and were a parallel to them in being overcome and subdued. But the first view is more preferred, because His saying ﴿not long ago﴾ implies that they were before them by a short period of time, and that applies more to Banu Qaynuqa'. Also, comparing Banu al-Nadir with Banu Qaynuqa' is more fitting, because they were Jews like them, and they were expelled from their homes just as was done to them. That is what is meant by His saying ﴿They tasted the bad consequence of their affair﴾. And qarIban (قريباً, "not long ago") is an adverb of time.

Ibn Juzayy, al-Tashil, on Surah 59, verses 16–17:

﴿Like the Shaytan (Satan) when he says to man, "Disbelieve."﴾ God gave the example of the hypocrites who misled the Jews of Banu al-Nadir, then abandoned them afterward, by means of Satan, for he misleads the son of Adam and then disowns him. The meaning of "Shaytan" and "man" here is the category (genus). It has also been said that he meant the Satan who misled the Quraysh on the day of Badr and said to them: ﴿"Indeed, I am your protector"﴾ [al-Anfal: 48]. ﴿"So the outcome of both of them will be that they are in the Fire."﴾ The two pronouns refer to Satan and man, and in this is an illustration of the hypocrites and the Jews.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 59, verse 18–19:

﴿And let every soul look to what it has sent forward for tomorrow.﴾ This is a command that every soul should consider what it has sent forward of its deeds for the Day of Resurrection. The meaning of this is the self-accounting (muhasabat al-nafs) so that it refrains from evil deeds and increases its good deeds. He expressed the Day of Resurrection as "tomorrow" (ghad) to bring it near, because everything that is coming is near. If it is said: why was the command to piety repeated? The answer is in two respects. One of them is that it is emphasis. The other, and it is the better one, is that He first commanded piety in preparation for the Day of Resurrection, then commanded it a second time because Allah is Aware of what they do. So when the reasons differed, He repeated it with each of them. ﴿And do not be like those who forgot Allah⦈ meaning the disbelievers. The forgetting (al-nisyan) here may mean abandonment (al-tark) or heedlessness (al-ghafla), i.e., they forgot the right of Allah, so He made them forget the rights of their own souls and the consideration of them.

The forgetting (al-nisyan) here may mean abandonment (al-tark) or heedlessness (al-ghafla), i.e., they forgot the right of Allah, so He made them forget the rights of their own souls and the consideration of them.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 59, verse 21:

﴿Had We sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain﴾ (and so on): a rebuke to the children of Adam for the hardness of their hearts and the scarcity of their humility when reciting the Qur'an. For if the mountain would humble itself and split apart were it to hear the Qur'an, then what do you think of the son of Adam?

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 59, verse 22:

﴿He is the Knower of the unseen and the seen﴾. That is, He knows what is hidden from the creatures and what they witness. It is said: "the unseen" is the Hereafter and "the seen" is this world; but the general meaning is better.

﴿Al-Quddus (the Most Holy)﴾ is derived from *taqdis* (sanctification), which means being exempt from the attributes of created beings and from every deficiency and defect. The pattern *fa'ul*, used for intensification (*mubalagha*), is as in *al-Subbuh* (the Most Glorified). ﴿Al-Salam (the Source of Peace)﴾ has two interpretations: one is that He is the One who has kept His servants safe from injustice, and the other is that He is free from all imperfections. Its origin is a *masdar* (verbal noun, here meaning "safety"), applied to Allah as an intensive description, or it is understood as elided, with the meaning "the Possessor of Peace." ﴿Al-Mu'min (the Giver of Security)﴾ has two interpretations: one is that it derives from *amn* (security), meaning He who grants security to His servants, and the other is that it derives from *iman* (faith), meaning He who confirms His servants in their faith, or who confirms their testimony about people on the Day of Resurrection, or who confirms Himself in His statements. ﴿Al-Muhaymin (the Guardian)﴾ has three interpretations: the Watchful, the Witness, and the Trustworthy. Al-Zamakhshari said: its origin is *mu'yamin* with a hamza, then the hamza was replaced by a *ha'*. ﴿Al-Jabbar (the Compeller)﴾ has two interpretations: one is that it derives from *ijbar* (compulsion) in the sense of subjugation, and the other is that it derives from *jabr* (restoration), meaning that He restores His servants by His mercy. The first is more apparent. ﴿Al-Mutakabbir (the Supreme in Greatness)﴾ means the One to whom greatness belongs in truth. ﴿Al-Bari' (the Evolver)﴾ means the Creator. It is said: "Allah *abra'a* the creation," meaning He created them. However, *al-Bari'* and *al-Fatir* are both intended to mean the One who brought creation into being and originated it. ﴿Al-Musawwir (the Fashioner)﴾ means the Creator of forms. ﴿To Him belong the Most Beautiful Names﴾.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed Allah has ninety-nine names; whoever counts them enters Paradise."

The author said: I recited the Qur'an to the righteous teacher Abu 'Abd Allah ibn al-Kammad, and when I reached the end of Surah al-Hashr, he said to me: "Put your hand on your head." I said to him: "Why is that?" He said: "Because I recited to the judge Abu 'Ali ibn Abi al-Ahwas, and when I reached the conclusion of al-Hashr he said to me: 'Put your hand on your head.' " And he traced the hadith back to 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, who said: "I recited to the Prophet ﷺ, and when I reached the conclusion of al-Hashr he said to me: 'Put your hand on your head.' I said: 'Why is that, O Messenger of Allah? May my father and mother be ransom for you.' He said: 'Jibril recited the Qur'an to me, and when I reached the conclusion of al-Hashr, he said to me: "Put your hand on your head, O Muhammad." I said: "Why is that?" He said: "Indeed Allah, blessed and exalted, opened the Qur'an and set forth its examples in it, and when He reached the end of Surah al-Hashr, He commanded the angels to place their hands upon their heads." They said: "O our Lord, why is that?" He said: "It is a cure for every ailment except *al-sam*, and *al-sam* is death.'"
